title: Hard experiences
hook: a 2020 review estimated about 8 percent of meditators report unpleasant effects (Farias et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mindfulness in schools: a big trial found required lessons no better than usual teaching. Your line was invite, don't force.

Not every sit ends in peace. Someone closes their eyes for a few minutes of breathing, and instead of quiet, their heart starts racing. Or an old memory they'd packed away comes up with full force. Or the room starts to feel strangely unreal. The cheerful version of meditation skips this part. But it belongs to the honest picture: sometimes practice is hard, and not in a good way. Today, what researchers found, what one old teacher wrote about his own breakdown, and how to know when to stop.
screen: `NOT EVERY SIT ENDS IN PEACE.` → `A RACING HEART, AN OLD MEMORY.` → `THE HONEST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the numbers, carefully. A review led by Miguel Farias pooled studies that asked meditators about unpleasant effects. It estimated that about 8 percent reported at least one; anxiety and low mood were among the most common. That's a minority. But it isn't zero, and it isn't nothing. Second, the old teachers knew. The Japanese Zen teacher Hakuin wrote about his own collapse in a text known as Idle Talk on a Night Boat. As he tells it, he pushed his practice so hard that his body and mind broke down, a condition he called Zen sickness; Zen has its own word for this. A hermit, he says, taught him a gentler practice that helped him recover. Third, the signs. Clinicians who study these experiences describe warning signs worth knowing: panic that builds rather than passes, feeling detached or unreal, painful memories flooding in, sleep falling apart. Their advice is plain: open your eyes, feel your feet, move your body, shorten the sit or stop, and talk to someone. If thoughts of harming yourself ever come, reach out right away: call your local emergency number, or in the US, call or text 988. Fourth, what stopping means. Stopping isn't failing. Hakuin's own story turns on learning a gentler way. Knowing your edge is part of the practice, not a break from it.
screen: `ABOUT 8 PERCENT REPORTED ONE.` · `HAKUIN'S ZEN SICKNESS.` · `PANIC, UNREALITY, FLOODING.` · `STOPPING ISN'T FAILING.` · then, large: `KNOW WHEN TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Keep your eyes open today, resting softly on the floor a little ahead of you, both feet on the ground, breathing normally. Gently ask what your own signs would be, a tight chest, a spinning head, feeling far away, and name one or two quietly. Then make the plan: if that comes, I open my eyes wide, look around the room, press my feet down, and stop.
Hard experiences. A minority of meditators report unpleasant effects, and old teachers wrote about them too. Today's word.
Your line: know when to stop. The way out is always right there, and using it is no failure. Take good care.

howItsDone: Careful meditation teachers ask students to notice warning signs such as panic, feeling unreal or flooding memories, and to open their eyes, ground themselves, shorten or stop practice, and seek help when those signs appear.
